Web Development.d: A way of running software projects in short cycles, delivering working pieces often and adjusting based on feedback rather than fixing every detail up front.
Web Development.why: You see progress early and can change priorities without restarting the project.

Web Development.d: A set of rules that lets one piece of software ask another for data or actions. When your website shows a map, takes a card payment or pulls in reviews, it is usually talking to another service through an API.
Web Development.why: APIs let you connect tools you already pay for instead of rebuilding them.

Web Development.d: Code that starts a task, such as loading data, and carries on with other work instead of waiting for it to finish.
Web Development.why: Async code keeps pages responsive while slower tasks run in the background.

Web Development.d: Checking who someone is, usually with a password, a code or a passkey, before letting them in.
Web Development.why: Strong sign-in protects customer accounts and your admin areas.

Web Development.d: Deciding what a signed-in person is allowed to see or do, such as whether they can edit pages or only view them.
Web Development.why: Limits the damage if one account is misused.

Web Development.d: The part of a website or app that runs on the server: databases, business logic, user accounts and anything the visitor does not see directly.
A saved copy of your site files and database that can be restored if something breaks, is hacked or is deleted by mistake.
Web Development.why: A tested, recent backup is the difference between a bad afternoon and losing your site.

Web Development.d: The program people use to view websites, such as Chrome, Safari, Edge or Firefox. Each one displays code slightly differently, so sites are tested in several.
A mistake in code that makes software behave in a way nobody intended.
The step that turns source code into the optimized files that are actually served to visitors, often bundling, minifying and checking the code along the way.
A stored copy of data or pages kept close at hand so they can be served faster the next time, without redoing the work.
Web Development.why: Good caching makes sites feel fast and lowers hosting load. Stale caches are also why changes sometimes do not show up right away.

Web Development.d: A network of servers around the world that stores copies of your site's files and serves each visitor from a nearby location.
Web Development.why: Faster loading for visitors far from your main server, plus extra protection against traffic spikes.

Web Development.d: Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery or Deployment: automated steps that test and release code every time a change is made.
Web Development.why: Fewer manual mistakes and quicker, safer updates.

Web Development.d: A text-based way to control software by typing commands instead of clicking buttons.
Building a page in the visitor's browser with JavaScript after the initial download, rather than on the server.
Web Development.why: Can feel app-like, but if done carelessly it can slow first loads and make content harder for search engines to read.

Web Development.d: A teammate reading proposed code changes before they go live to catch bugs, security issues and confusing code.
A lightweight package that bundles an application with everything it needs to run, so it behaves the same on a laptop, a test server and production. Docker is the best-known tool.
Software that lets non-developers create and edit website content through an admin screen.
Web Development.why: Your team can update the site without calling a developer for every change.

Web Development.d: A small piece of data a website stores in the browser to remember things like a login, a cart or preferences.
Web Development.why: Some cookies need visitor consent under privacy laws, so your site may need a consent banner.

Web Development.d: A browser security rule that controls which other websites are allowed to request data from your server.
A task scheduled to run automatically at set times, such as a nightly backup or a weekly report.
Checking that a site looks and works correctly across different browsers and devices.
Create, Read, Update, Delete: the four basic things most apps do with data.
The language that controls how web pages look: colors, fonts, spacing and layout.
An organized store of information, such as products, orders or users, that an app can search and update quickly.
Finding and fixing the cause of a bug.
An outside library or package your code relies on.
Web Development.why: Outdated dependencies are a common source of security holes, so they need regular updates.

Web Development.d: Putting a new version of a site or app live on a server so people can use it.
The plan and tools for getting systems running again after a serious failure, attack or data loss.
Web Development.why: Knowing how long recovery takes helps you judge how much downtime you can live with.

Web Development.d: The internet's address book. It turns a domain like example.com into the numeric address of the server that hosts it.
Web Development.why: DNS settings control where your website and email go, so mistakes here can take both offline.

Web Development.d: A popular tool for creating and running containers.
The browser's live, structured model of a web page, which JavaScript reads and changes to update what you see.
The human-readable address of a website, such as tenshi.example. You rent it yearly from a registrar.
Web Development.why: Register it in your company's name and turn on auto-renew so it cannot lapse.

Web Development.d: Running code on servers close to the visitor, often inside a CDN, instead of in one central data center.
Web Development.why: Lower delay for visitors spread across regions.

Web Development.d: Scrambling data so only someone with the right key can read it. HTTPS encrypts data in transit; disk or database encryption protects data at rest.
Settings, such as API keys or database addresses, kept outside the code so they can differ between test and live systems and stay out of public view.
Web Development.why: Keeps secrets out of your code repository.

Web Development.d: A filter that blocks unwanted network traffic. A web application firewall (WAF) specifically screens website requests for common attacks.
A ready-made structure and toolkit for building software, such as React-based Next.js, Laravel or Django, so developers do not start from scratch.
Everything visitors see and interact with in the browser: layout, buttons, forms and animations.
Work, or a developer, covering both the front end and the back end.
The most widely used version control system. It records every change to code and lets teams work on the same project safely.
A website for hosting Git repositories, reviewing code and running automation. It can also host simple static websites.
A way of building APIs where the app asks for exactly the fields it needs in one request.
A content management system that stores and edits content but leaves the display to a separate front end, connected through an API.
Web Development.why: Lets you reuse the same content on a website, an app and elsewhere.

Web Development.d: Renting space on a server so your website is available on the internet around the clock.
The language that structures web page content into headings, paragraphs, links, images and forms.
The protocol browsers and servers use to request and send web pages.
The secure, encrypted version of HTTP, shown by the padlock in the browser.
Web Development.why: Browsers warn visitors about sites without it, and it protects any data people send you.

Web Development.d: A code editor with built-in tools for writing, running and debugging code.
An approach that serves pre-built pages from a CDN and adds dynamic features through JavaScript and APIs.
Web Development.why: Often fast, secure and cheap to host.

Web Development.d: The programming language that runs in web browsers and makes pages interactive. It also runs on servers through Node.js.
A simple text format for structured data that is easy for both people and programs to read. Most APIs send data as JSON.
Waiting to load images or other content until the visitor is about to scroll to them.
Web Development.why: Speeds up the first view of a page.

Web Development.d: A collection of ready-made code for a specific job, such as handling dates or drawing charts, that developers plug into a project.
A system that spreads incoming traffic across several servers so no single one is overwhelmed.
A developer's own computer acting as a private web server for building and testing before anything goes live.
An architecture where an app is split into many small, independent services that talk to each other through APIs.
Web Development.why: Can help large systems scale, but adds complexity most small projects do not need.

Web Development.d: Software that sits between parts of a system, such as checking logins or logging requests before they reach the main app.
Removing spaces, comments and long names from code files to make them smaller and faster to download.
An app built and deployed as one single unit. Simpler to run than microservices and often the right choice for small teams.
The simplest version of a product that solves the core problem well enough to test with real users.
Web Development.why: Lets you learn what customers want before spending heavily.

Web Development.d: A runtime that lets JavaScript run on servers, widely used for back ends and developer tooling.
Software whose source code is public and can be used, changed and shared under its license.
Web Development.why: Can lower costs, but check the license and that the project is actively maintained.

Web Development.d: A tool that lets developers work with database records as normal code objects instead of writing raw SQL.
A tool, such as npm, that installs and updates the libraries a project depends on.
A server-side programming language that powers WordPress and many other websites.
A website that behaves like an app: it can be installed on a home screen, load quickly and sometimes work offline.
Web Development.why: App-like convenience without app store fees or separate builds.

Web Development.d: A proposed set of code changes submitted for review before being merged into the main code.
A readable, general-purpose programming language popular for back ends, automation, data work and AI.
Capping how many requests someone can make in a set time, to stop abuse and keep a service stable.
A popular JavaScript library for building interactive user interfaces from reusable components.
The storage place for a project's code and its full change history.
A common style of API that uses standard web addresses and HTTP methods to read and change data.
Returning a site or app to its previous working version after a bad update.
A bundle of tools, code and documentation that makes it easier to build on a particular platform or API.
An update that fixes a known security weakness in software.
Web Development.why: Applying patches promptly is one of the cheapest ways to avoid being hacked.

Web Development.d: A computer that stores websites, apps or data and responds to requests from browsers and other software.
Building the full page on the server before sending it, so visitors and search engines receive ready-to-read content.
Web Development.why: Often helps first-load speed and search visibility.

Web Development.d: Running code on a cloud provider's infrastructure that starts on demand, so you do not manage servers yourself and usually pay only for what you use.
A background script that lets a website cache files, work offline and send notifications.
A temporary record that keeps a visitor signed in or remembers their cart as they move between pages.
A website that loads once and then updates content in place as you click, without full page reloads.
Structured Query Language, the standard language for asking questions of and updating relational databases.
A digital certificate that proves your site's identity and enables HTTPS encryption. TLS is the modern successor to SSL, though both names are used.
Web Development.why: Needed for the browser padlock; many hosts provide free certificates that renew automatically.

Web Development.d: A private copy of your live site used to test changes before visitors see them.
Web Development.why: Catches problems before they reach customers.

Web Development.d: A website made of pre-built files served the same way to every visitor, without a database building each page on request.
Web Development.why: Typically fast, secure and inexpensive to host.

Web Development.d: A tool that turns templates and content into a complete static website at build time.
A three-digit number a server returns with each response, such as 200 for OK, 301 for moved permanently or 404 for not found.
The future cost of shortcuts taken in code today, which make later changes slower and riskier.
Web Development.why: Some debt is fine, but unmanaged debt makes every new feature cost more.

Web Development.d: Checking that software works as intended, often with automated tests that run on every change. Unit tests check small pieces; end-to-end tests check whole user journeys.
Signing in with a second proof, such as a code from an app, in addition to a password.
Web Development.why: Turn it on for your hosting, domain, email and admin accounts.

Web Development.d: JavaScript with added type checking, which catches many mistakes before code runs.
The share of time a site or service is available and working.
A service that regularly checks your site and alerts you when it goes down.
The full web address of a specific page or file, such as https://example.com/about.
A system that tracks every change to code so teams can collaborate, review history and undo mistakes.
A virtual server with its own guaranteed share of a physical machine, giving more control than shared hosting.
Software, such as Nginx or Apache, that receives browser requests and sends back pages and files.
An automatic message one app sends to another the moment something happens, such as a new order or payment.
Web Development.why: Lets tools react instantly without someone copying data across.

Web Development.d: A connection that stays open between browser and server so data can flow both ways instantly, used for chat and live updates.
A widely used open-source content management system written in PHP, extended with themes and plugins.
Web Development.why: Flexible and familiar, but plugins and core need regular updates to stay secure.

Web Design.d: Showing two versions of a page or element to different visitors and measuring which performs better against a goal.
Web Design.why: Replaces guesswork with evidence from your own visitors.

Web Design.d: The part of a page visible before scrolling. The term comes from the top half of a folded newspaper.
Web Design.why: Your main message and next step should be clear here.

Web Design.d: Designing and building so people with disabilities, including those using screen readers, keyboards or magnification, can use your site.
Web Design.why: Widens your audience, improves usability for everyone and is a legal requirement in many places.

Web Design.d: A visual clue that suggests how something is used, such as a button that looks pressable.
A short written description of an image, read aloud by screen readers and shown if the image fails to load.
Web Design.why: Helps accessibility and helps search engines understand your images.

Web Design.d: The proportion of an image's or video's width to its height, such as 16:9 or 1:1.
A document setting out how your logo, colors, fonts, imagery and voice should be used.
Web Design.why: Keeps every page, post and print piece consistent.

Web Design.d: The visible and verbal elements that make your business recognizable: name, logo, colors, type and tone.
The consistent personality and tone in your writing, such as warm and plain-spoken or formal and technical.
A small trail of links, such as Home > Services > Web Design, showing where a page sits in the site.
Web Design.why: Helps visitors and search engines understand your site structure.

Web Design.d: A screen width at which a responsive layout changes, for example from one column on phones to three on desktops.
A prompt that asks the visitor to take the next step, such as Book a call or Get a quote.
Web Design.why: Every key page should make the next step obvious.

Web Design.d: A boxed block that groups an image, a title and a short summary, often arranged in grids.
A research method where people group topics into categories, used to shape navigation and labels.
A rotating set of slides or images in one space.
Web Design.why: Visitors often miss slides after the first, so put the most important message somewhere static.

Web Design.d: The difference in brightness between text and its background. WCAG sets minimum contrast ratios for readable text.
The defined set of colors a brand or site uses, usually with primary, secondary and neutral shades.
The share of visitors who complete a goal you care about, such as sending an inquiry, booking a call or buying.
Web Design.why: Improving it gets more results from the traffic you already have.

Web Design.d: A color scheme with light text on a dark background, often following the visitor's device setting.
A shared library of reusable components, patterns and rules, with guidance on how to use them.
Web Design.why: Speeds up design and development and keeps products consistent as they grow.

Web Design.d: A menu that reveals a list of options when clicked or hovered.
A common way people scan text-heavy pages: across the top, then down the left side, glancing right.
Web Design.why: Put key words at the start of headings and lines.

Web Design.d: The small icon shown in the browser tab, bookmarks and sometimes search results.
A popular browser-based tool for designing interfaces, wireframes and prototypes collaboratively.
A clean style that avoids heavy shadows, textures and 3D effects in favor of simple shapes and color.
Choosing typefaces that work well together, often one for headings and another for body text.
The bottom area of a site, usually holding contact details, key links, legal pages and social links.
Laying out forms so they are quick and clear to complete: few fields, clear labels and helpful error messages.
Web Design.why: Every unnecessary field can cost you inquiries.

Web Design.d: Psychology-based rules about how people group what they see, such as items placed close together being seen as related.
An invisible set of columns and gutters used to align content consistently.
The three-line icon that opens a hidden menu, common on mobile.
The top area of a site, usually holding the logo and main navigation.
A visual overlay showing where visitors click, move or scroll on a page.
Web Design.why: Shows what people actually notice and ignore.

Web Design.d: The large opening area at the top of a page, usually with a headline, a short message, an image and a call to action.
A six-character code, such as #1A2B3C, that defines a color on the web.
The set of icons used across a site and their consistent style.
Resizing and compressing images, and using modern formats such as WebP or AVIF, so they load quickly without looking worse.
Web Design.why: Images are often the heaviest part of a page.

Web Design.d: How content is organized, labeled and connected so people can find what they need.
Adjusting the space between specific pairs of letters.
A focused page built for one goal, often the destination for an ad or campaign.
The arrangement of text, images and other elements on a page.
The vertical space between lines of text, also called line height.
The graphic mark or wordmark that identifies your business.
The small bits of text in an interface, such as button labels, hints and error messages.
Web Design.why: Clear microcopy reduces confusion and support questions.

Web Design.d: A small animated response to an action, such as a button changing when pressed.
A design approach that strips away anything unnecessary so key content stands out.
Designing for small screens first, then expanding the layout for larger screens.
Web Design.why: Many visitors arrive on phones, and search engines evaluate the mobile version of your site.

Web Design.d: A static, realistic picture of what a page will look like, more detailed than a wireframe.
A window that appears over the page and requires interaction before returning to the content.
A collage of images, colors and type that sets the visual direction before design starts.
The menus and links that help visitors move around a site.
An effect where background and foreground move at different speeds as you scroll.
Web Design.why: Use lightly; heavy effects can slow pages and bother some visitors.

Web Design.d: A research-based profile of a typical customer, describing goals, needs and frustrations.
Web Design.why: Keeps design decisions focused on real customers.

Web Design.d: A box that appears over content, often to collect emails or show offers.
Web Design.why: Intrusive pop-ups annoy visitors, especially on mobile.

Web Design.d: A clickable model of a site or app used to test ideas before building.
How easy text is to read and understand, shaped by wording, font size, line length and contrast.
Building pages that adapt their layout to any screen size.
A high-density screen, also called high-DPI, that needs sharper images to avoid looking blurry.
RGB is the color model used for screens; CMYK is used for printing.
Web Design.why: Your brand colors need both versions to look consistent online and in print.

Web Design.d: A typeface without small strokes at the ends of letters.
A typeface with small strokes at the ends of letters.
A plan of all a site's pages and how they relate. Designers use visual sitemaps for planning; search engines use XML sitemaps.
A gray placeholder outline shown while content loads.
Web Design.why: Makes waiting feel shorter.

Web Design.d: Signals that others trust you, such as reviews, case studies and client logos.
Web Design.why: Only use genuine reviews and real clients.

Web Design.d: A header that stays at the top of the screen while scrolling.
A reference for visual and writing standards, often part of brand guidelines or a design system.
Scalable Vector Graphics, a format for logos, icons and illustrations that stay crisp at any size.
A reusable page layout or design starting point.
A packaged design for a platform like WordPress or Shopify that controls the look of the whole site.
Elements that reassure visitors, such as clear contact details, HTTPS, privacy policies and real reviews.
A family of type designs, such as Helvetica. A font is one specific style within it, such as Helvetica Bold.
The art of arranging type: choosing typefaces, sizes, spacing and hierarchy.
The parts of a site or app people see and interact with: buttons, menus, forms and screens.
How easily people can use something to reach their goals.
Watching real people try tasks on your site to find where they get stuck.
Web Design.why: A few sessions often reveal problems your team cannot see.

Web Design.d: Tools that record anonymized clicks, scrolls and session replays to show how people use a site.
The steps a visitor takes to complete a task, such as from product page to checkout.
The full path a customer takes with your business, from first hearing of you to buying and returning.
How it feels to use a product or site overall: ease, clarity, speed and satisfaction.
Images defined by shapes and math rather than pixels, so they scale without losing quality. Raster images, like photos, are made of pixels.
Arranging elements by size, color, contrast and position so people notice the most important things first.
The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, the international standard for web accessibility, with levels A, AA and AAA.
Web Design.why: Many laws and contracts reference WCAG Level AA.

Web Design.d: Fonts loaded from the web so text looks the same on every device.
Web Design.why: Too many font files can slow a page down.

Web Design.d: Empty space around and between elements, also called negative space.
Web Design.why: Makes pages calmer and easier to scan.

Web Design.d: A simple black-and-white sketch of a page's structure, without final visuals.

SEO.d: A permanent redirect that sends visitors and search engines from an old URL to a new one.
SEO.why: Keeps the search value of old pages when you move or rename them.

SEO.d: A temporary redirect, used when a page will come back to its original URL.
The not-found response shown when a page does not exist.
SEO.why: A helpful custom 404 page keeps lost visitors on your site.

SEO.d: Google's AI-generated summaries that can appear at the top of some search results, with links to sources.
The rules and calculations a search engine uses to decide which pages to show and in what order.
The clickable words of a link.
SEO.why: Descriptive anchor text helps people and search engines know what the linked page is about.

SEO.d: A link from another website to yours.
SEO.why: Links from relevant, reputable sites are a strong trust signal for search engines.

SEO.d: Tactics that try to trick search engines, such as hidden text or paid link schemes, against search engine guidelines.
SEO.why: Can lead to penalties that are slow to recover from.

SEO.d: The share of visits where someone leaves without engaging further. Definitions vary between analytics tools.
Structured data that tells search engines a page's breadcrumb trail, which can show in search results.
A tag that tells search engines which version of similar or duplicate pages is the main one.
The share of people who click a result or ad after seeing it.
SEO.why: Clear titles and descriptions can earn more clicks from the same rankings.

SEO.d: Attracting customers by publishing genuinely useful content such as articles, guides and videos.
Google's set of metrics for real-world page experience: loading (Largest Contentful Paint), responsiveness (Interaction to Next Paint) and visual stability (Cumulative Layout Shift).
SEO.why: Faster, steadier pages help both visitors and search performance.

SEO.d: Roughly how many pages a search engine will crawl on your site in a given time. Mostly a concern for very large sites.
A problem that stops a search engine reaching a page, such as a broken link or server error.
A program, also called a bot or spider, that search engines use to discover and read web pages.
A Core Web Vitals metric measuring how much content unexpectedly jumps around while a page loads.
A third-party score estimating how strong a site's backlink profile is. It is a vendor metric, not something Google uses.
The same or very similar content appearing at more than one URL.
Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness and Trustworthiness: qualities Google's quality rater guidelines use to describe helpful, reliable content.
SEO.why: Show real experience, named authors and clear contact details.

SEO.d: In Google Analytics 4, the share of sessions where someone engaged meaningfully, for example by staying a while or viewing more than one page.
Content that stays useful for a long time rather than going out of date quickly.
A highlighted answer shown at the top of some search results, pulled from a web page.
Making content easy for AI-powered search and assistants to understand, trust and cite. Much of it overlaps with good SEO: clear, accurate, well-structured content.
Google's free tool for measuring website traffic and visitor behavior. The current version is Google Analytics 4 (GA4).
Your free business listing on Google Search and Maps, showing hours, location, photos and reviews.
SEO.why: Essential for local customers finding you.

SEO.d: Google's free tool showing how your site performs in search, which pages are indexed and any problems found.
HTML tags from H1 to H6 that structure a page's headings. Usually one H1 states the page's main topic.
SEO.why: Clear headings help readers scan and help search engines understand your content.

SEO.d: Content written for people first, that fully answers their question, rather than content made mainly to rank.
A tag telling search engines which language or region each version of a page is for.
SEO.why: Important for sites in more than one language, such as Japanese and English.

SEO.d: Helping images appear in search through descriptive file names, alt text, sensible sizes and surrounding text.
How many times your page appeared in search results, whether or not anyone clicked.
A search engine storing a page in its database so it can appear in results.
A Core Web Vitals metric measuring how quickly a page responds to clicks, taps and key presses.
A link from one page on your site to another.
SEO.why: Guides visitors and spreads search value across your pages.

SEO.d: A word or phrase people type into a search engine.
A third-party estimate of how hard it would be to rank for a keyword.
Finding the words and phrases your customers actually use when searching.
Cramming keywords unnaturally into content. It hurts readability and goes against search guidelines.
An information box in search results about a business, person or thing.
A Core Web Vitals metric measuring how long the main content of a page takes to appear.
A free Google tool that audits a page's performance, accessibility, best practices and SEO.
Earning links from other reputable websites, for example through useful content, partnerships or PR.
SEO.why: Earned links last; bought links risk penalties.

SEO.d: Improving visibility in searches with local intent, such as web designer in Osaka.
A longer, more specific search phrase. Fewer people search for it, but they often know exactly what they want.
A short page summary in the HTML that search engines may show under your title in results.
SEO.why: Doesn't directly lift rankings, but a good one can win more clicks.

SEO.d: Google mainly uses the mobile version of a site's content for indexing and ranking.
Optimizing a site in several languages so each version is found by the right audience.
Keeping your business Name, Address and Phone number identical across your site and online listings.
A link attribute asking search engines not to pass ranking credit through a link. Related values mark sponsored and user-generated links.
An instruction telling search engines not to include a page in results.
Work done outside your site to build its reputation, such as earning links and reviews.
Improving the content and HTML of your own pages, such as titles, headings, text and internal links.
Visitors who arrive from unpaid search results.
A page with no internal links pointing to it, so visitors and crawlers struggle to find it.
Google's broader view of how pleasant a page is to use, including Core Web Vitals, HTTPS and avoiding intrusive pop-ups.
How quickly a page loads and becomes usable.
SEO.why: Slow pages lose visitors and inquiries.

SEO.d: A free Google tool that reports a page's speed and Core Web Vitals, with suggestions.
Ads that appear in search results, usually paid per click.
A comprehensive page on a broad topic that links to more detailed related articles.
Something a search engine considers when ordering results. Search engines do not publish full lists or weights.
Several redirects in a row before reaching the final page, which slows visitors and crawlers.
Visitors who arrive by clicking a link on another website.
Customer ratings and comments on platforms such as Google.
SEO.why: Real reviews influence choices and local visibility. Never fake or buy them.

SEO.d: Enhanced search listings with extras such as star ratings, prices or FAQs, often enabled by structured data.
A file at the root of your site telling crawlers which areas they may visit.
SEO.why: A wrong line here can hide a whole site from search.

SEO.d: Structured data code, usually from the Schema.org vocabulary, that labels content such as businesses, products, events and articles for search engines.
The goal behind a search: to learn something, find a site, compare options or buy.
SEO.why: Match each page to the intent behind its keywords.

SEO.d: An estimate of how often a keyword is searched in a period.
Getting visibility in search engines, usually meaning paid ads, sometimes including SEO.
Improving a website so it appears more often, and higher, in unpaid search results for relevant searches.
Search Engine Results Page: the page of results shown after a search.
How a site's pages are organized and linked together.
The readable end part of a URL that identifies a page, such as /web-design-services.
Information formatted in a standard way so machines can understand it. On the web it usually means schema markup.
Making sure search engines can crawl, render and index a site, covering speed, sitemaps, redirects and code.
Pages with little useful content.
The HTML title of a page, usually shown as the clickable headline in search results and in the browser tab.
A group of related articles linked to a central pillar page, covering a subject thoroughly.
Tags added to a link, such as ?utm_source=newsletter, so analytics can show which campaign brought visitors.
Searching by speaking to a phone or smart speaker, often using longer, question-style phrases.
Ethical SEO that follows search engine guidelines and focuses on real value for people.
A file listing your important pages to help search engines find them.
A search where the person gets their answer on the results page and does not click any website.

SaaS.d: The moment a new user first gets real value from a product.
SaaS.why: Users who reach it early are more likely to stay.

SaaS.d: The back-office area where account owners manage settings, users and billing.
A subscription paid yearly, often discounted compared with paying monthly.
Japan's Act on the Protection of Personal Information, the main law governing how businesses handle personal data in Japan.
SaaS.why: Affects how you collect, store and share customer data in Japan. Get legal advice for specifics.

SaaS.d: Revenue divided by the number of users or accounts over a period.
The yearly value of active subscriptions, excluding one-off fees.
A record of who did what and when inside a system.
SaaS.why: Helps with security investigations and compliance.

SaaS.d: Business to business: selling to other companies.
Business to consumer: selling directly to individuals.
The prioritized list of features, fixes and tasks waiting to be worked on.
A pre-release version shared with selected users to find problems before full launch.
How often a subscription is charged, such as monthly or yearly.
A running record of product updates and fixes.
The rate at which customers cancel or revenue is lost over a period.
SaaS.why: Small monthly churn compounds into big annual losses.

SaaS.d: Using computing power, storage and software over the internet from a provider instead of owning the hardware.
A group of customers who share a starting point, such as signing up in the same month, tracked over time.
Offering a related product to an existing customer.
A survey score measuring how satisfied customers are with a specific interaction or product.
The total sales and marketing cost to win one new customer.
The total revenue or profit you expect from a customer over the whole relationship.
SaaS.why: Compare it with acquisition cost to judge if growth is profitable.

SaaS.d: A team or practice focused on helping customers achieve their goals with your product, which reduces churn.
A screen that summarizes key information and metrics at a glance.
The ability to download your data from a service in a usable format.
SaaS.why: Check this before signing up so you are never trapped.

SaaS.d: Where data is physically stored, which can matter for legal and contractual rules.
Daily active users divided by monthly active users, a common measure of how habitually people use a product.
Moving a customer to a cheaper plan.
The process of retrying failed payments and reminding customers to update their card.
SaaS.why: Reduces involuntary churn from expired cards.

SaaS.term: Encryption at rest and in transit
SaaS.d: Protecting stored data (at rest) and data moving between systems (in transit) by encrypting it.
Extra revenue from existing customers through upgrades, more seats or add-ons.
A switch that turns a feature on or off for some users without releasing new code.
SaaS.why: Allows safe testing and gradual rollouts.

SaaS.d: A suggestion from a customer for something new.
Full or partial access for a limited time before paying.
A model offering a free plan with limits, with paid plans for more features or usage.
The EU's General Data Protection Regulation, which governs how personal data of people in the EU is handled. It can apply to businesses outside the EU.
The plan for how a product reaches customers: audience, pricing, channels and messaging.
Software for managing customer support requests.
Software that serves many industries with a common need, such as accounting or email marketing.
Infrastructure as a Service: renting raw computing resources like servers and storage from a cloud provider.
A connection that lets two software products share data or trigger actions in each other.
A bill listing what a customer owes and when.
Integration Platform as a Service: tools that connect apps and automate workflows between them without much code.
A searchable library of help articles and guides for customers or staff.
SaaS.why: Answers common questions around the clock and reduces support load.

SaaS.d: Platforms that let people build apps or automations with visual tools and little or no programming.
SaaS.why: Quick for simple needs; check limits, costs and data export before you rely on one.

SaaS.d: A small, focused software product, often run by a tiny team, serving a narrow need.
The predictable monthly revenue from active subscriptions.
Requiring two or more proofs of identity to sign in.
An architecture where many customers share the same software and infrastructure while their data is kept separate.
SaaS.why: Usually lowers costs and makes updates easier for everyone.

SaaS.d: Revenue kept from a group of existing customers over a period, including upgrades and minus churn and downgrades.
A survey metric based on how likely customers are to recommend you, on a 0 to 10 scale.
The process of helping new users set up and start getting value quickly.
Platform as a Service: a managed platform for running your own apps without managing servers.
Paying only for what you use, with no fixed commitment.
How long it takes for a customer's revenue to cover the cost of acquiring them.
A service that securely processes online card and wallet payments.
A barrier that limits access to content or features until someone pays.
The Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard, security rules for any business handling card data.
SaaS.why: Using a reputable payment gateway greatly reduces what you must handle yourself.

SaaS.d: Charging per user who has access.
A strategy where the product itself, through trials and self-serve sign-up, drives acquisition and expansion.
When a product clearly meets the needs of a market that is willing to pay for it.
Adjusting a charge for the part of a billing period used when a plan changes.
A summary of what changed in a specific version.
The share of customers who keep using or paying for a product over time.
A plan of upcoming features and priorities over time.
Giving permissions based on a person's role, such as admin, editor or viewer.
Software you use through the internet on a subscription, instead of installing and maintaining it yourself.
A safe test environment where you can try features or integrations without affecting real data.
How well a system handles growth in users, data or traffic without breaking or slowing down.
Customers can sign up, pay and manage their account without talking to sales.
A contract term defining promised service levels, such as uptime or support response time, and what happens if they are missed.
Signing in once with one account, such as a company Google or Microsoft account, to access several apps.
SaaS.why: Easier for staff and simpler to remove access when someone leaves.

SaaS.d: An architecture where each customer gets their own separate instance of the software.
An auditing framework, from the AICPA, for how a service provider protects customer data. Common in B2B software buying.
see: Encryption at rest and in transit

SaaS.d: A short, fixed period, often one to four weeks, in which a team completes a set of work.
How often users return to a product, often measured by DAU/MAU.
Paying regularly, monthly or yearly, for ongoing access.
One customer's account and data within a multi-tenant system.
A single customer support request tracked in a help desk.
Plans at different price points with different features or limits.
The full cost of a tool over time, including subscription, setup, training, integration and switching costs.
Moving a customer to a higher plan.
Encouraging a customer to buy a higher plan or add more.
Charging based on consumption, such as messages sent or storage used.
A short description of a feature from the user's point of view, such as As a shop owner, I want to export orders so that I can do my accounts.
Being so dependent on one provider that switching becomes difficult or costly.
Software built for one specific industry, such as restaurants, clinics or real estate.
A product made by one company and rebranded and sold by another as its own.
Using software to carry out routine steps automatically, such as sending a welcome email when a form is submitted.

AI.d: A process in which an AI system plans and carries out several steps toward a goal, using tools along the way, rather than answering a single question.
An AI system that can take actions, such as searching, filling forms or calling APIs, to complete a task with some independence.
AI.why: Can handle routine multi-step work, but needs clear limits and human checks on important actions.

AI.d: Principles for building and using AI fairly, safely, transparently and with respect for privacy.
Search experiences where AI writes an answer from several sources instead of only listing links.
A step-by-step set of instructions for solving a problem. In AI, algorithms are used to learn patterns from data.
A hypothetical AI that could match humans across almost any intellectual task. There is no agreed definition or test for it.
Computer systems that perform tasks normally needing human intelligence, such as understanding language, recognizing images or making predictions.
A standard test used to compare AI models on specific tasks.
AI.why: Benchmarks rarely match your real work; test models on your own examples.

AI.d: Systematic unfairness in AI output, often inherited from skewed or incomplete training data.
AI.why: Can harm customers and your reputation; review outputs in sensitive areas such as hiring or lending.

AI.d: Having a model work through intermediate reasoning steps before giving an answer, which can improve results on complex problems.
Software that holds a conversation with people through text or voice. Modern chatbots are often powered by large language models.
AI.why: Can answer common questions instantly, but needs clear limits and an easy route to a human.

AI.d: An AI task that sorts items into categories, such as spam or not spam.
AI that interprets images and video, such as recognizing objects, reading text or inspecting products.
The maximum amount of text, measured in tokens, a model can consider at once, including your prompt, documents and its reply.
An AI assistant built into a tool to help people as they work, such as suggesting code or drafting emails.
Labeling data, such as tagging images or classifying text, so it can be used to train or test models.
Machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers. It powers most modern AI.
AI-generated or altered audio, images or video that realistically imitate a real person.
AI.why: Be wary of urgent payment requests by voice or video, and verify through another channel.

AI.d: A type of generative model, common in image generation, that creates images by gradually turning random noise into a picture.
A list of numbers representing the meaning of text, images or other data, so similar things end up close together.
AI.why: Powers smart search and recommendations over your own content.

AI.d: Systematically testing an AI system's quality on examples that reflect real use.
AI.why: The only reliable way to know whether an AI feature works for your business.

AI.d: How well people can understand why an AI system produced a particular output.
Giving a model a few examples in the prompt to show the pattern you want.
Further training an existing model on your own examples to specialize its behavior or style.
AI.why: Often unnecessary; good prompts and retrieval usually come first.

AI.d: A large model trained on broad data that can be adapted to many tasks.
A model's ability to request that a specific function or API be run with structured inputs. Often called tool use.
AI that creates new content, such as text, images, audio, code or video, based on patterns learned from data.
A chip originally built for graphics that is very good at the parallel math AI needs for training and inference.
Connecting a model's answers to trusted sources, such as your documents or the web, so responses are based on facts.
AI.why: Reduces made-up answers.

AI.d: Rules and checks that keep an AI system's behavior within safe, intended limits.
When an AI states something false or invented with confidence.
AI.why: Always check AI output for facts, figures and citations before publishing.

AI.d: A design where people review or approve AI decisions at key points.
AI.why: Keeps quality and accountability in your hands.

AI.d: Creating images from text descriptions or other images using AI.
AI.why: Check usage rights and label AI images where appropriate.

AI.d: Running a trained model to produce an output, such as answering a question.
The date after which a model has no information from its training data.
AI.why: For current facts, the model needs search or your own documents.

AI.d: A model trained on large amounts of text to understand and generate language.
The delay between sending a request and getting a response.
A branch of AI where systems learn patterns from data instead of following hand-written rules.
Automatically translating text between languages with AI.
AI.why: Useful for drafts, but have important customer-facing text checked by a fluent speaker.

AI.d: The trained system that takes inputs and produces outputs, such as predictions or text.
An open standard for connecting AI assistants to tools and data sources in a consistent way.
A model that can work with more than one kind of input or output, such as text, images and audio.
The field of AI concerned with understanding and producing human language.
A computing system loosely inspired by the brain, made of layers of connected nodes that learn from data.
Technology that turns text in images or scanned documents into editable text.
AI.why: Automates data entry from receipts, invoices and forms.

AI.d: AI that runs directly on a phone or computer rather than in the cloud.
AI.why: Can be faster and keep data on the device.

AI.d: A model whose trained parameters are published so others can run or adapt it, subject to its license.
When a model learns its training data too closely and performs poorly on new data.
The internal values a model learns during training. Model size is often described by its number of parameters.
Using data and models to forecast outcomes, such as demand or which customers may cancel.
The instructions and content you give an AI model.
Crafting prompts to get more accurate, useful results, for example by giving context, examples and a clear format.
An attack where hidden instructions in text, web pages or documents try to make an AI ignore its rules.
AI.why: A key risk when AI reads outside content or can take actions.

AI.d: A model designed to spend more computation thinking through a problem step by step before answering.
A system that suggests products or content based on behavior and similarities.
Training an AI by rewarding good outcomes and penalizing bad ones as it acts.
Developing and using AI with attention to safety, fairness, privacy, transparency and accountability.
A technique where the system first finds relevant information, such as from your documents, and gives it to the model to use when answering.
AI.why: Lets AI answer from your own up-to-date content.

AI.d: Reinforcement learning from human feedback: refining a model using people's ratings of its answers.
Using AI to judge whether text expresses positive, negative or neutral feeling.
AI.why: Helps you understand reviews and feedback at scale.

AI.d: A compact language model that is cheaper and faster to run, sometimes on-device, often for narrower tasks.
Converting spoken audio into written text.
Using AI to condense long text into the key points.
Training a model on labeled examples where the right answer is known.
Artificially generated data used to train or test models, often when real data is scarce or sensitive.
Background instructions that set an AI assistant's role, tone and rules before the conversation starts.
A setting that controls how random or predictable a model's outputs are. Lower is more consistent; higher is more varied.
Converting written text into natural-sounding speech.
A chunk of text, often part of a word, that a language model reads and writes. Usage and limits are often counted in tokens.
An AI model's ability to use external tools, such as search, calculators or APIs, to complete tasks.
The process of teaching a model by adjusting its parameters using data.
The examples a model learns from.
AI.why: Quality, rights and privacy of data matter.

AI.d: The neural network architecture behind most modern language models, built around a mechanism called attention.
Training a model to find patterns in data without labeled answers, such as grouping similar customers.
A database designed to store embeddings and quickly find the most similar items.
Asking a model to do a task with no examples, relying on its general training.
